```{r, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, results='hide'}
library(tidyverse)

options(mc.cores = parallel::detectCores())

 ### Import the dataset

```{r}
data <- read_xlsx(path = "/Users/pacoalvarez/Desktop/Diabetes/bpd_consensus.xlsx",
                  col_names = TRUE, na = "")
```

We can observe that there are two main outcomes in this analysis: `Systolic blood pressure` and `Diastolic blood pressure`. Both outcomes are going to be meta-analysed separetely. Thus, we are going to create two different subsets corresponding to both outcomes.

```{r}
# Systolic blood pressure subset
sys.data <- data %>%
  filter(outcome == "Systolic blood pressure")

# Diastolic blood pressure subset
dias.data <- data %>%
  filter(outcome == "Diastolic blood pressure")
```

#### Data inspection and wrangling

Observing the names of the different physical activity modalities (integrated in the `trt` column), we caught that we have to make a bit of data processing.

```{r}
# see all the physical activity modalities
unique(data$trt)

# data processing: modification in the general dataset and consequent subsetting
data <- data %>%
  mutate(trt = ifelse(trt == "mixed aerobic exercises", "Mixed aerobic exercises", trt)) %>%
  mutate(trt = ifelse(trt == "Resistance exercises", "Resistance", trt)) %>%
  mutate(trt = ifelse(trt == "Aerobic + Resistance exercises", "Aerobic + Resistance", trt)) %>%
  mutate(trt = ifelse(trt == "Mind-body training", "Mind-body", trt))

# Systolic blood pressure subset
sys.data <- data %>%
  filter(outcome == "Systolic blood pressure")

# Diastolic blood pressure subset
dias.data <- data %>%
  filter(outcome == "Diastolic blood pressure")
```

After that, trying conducting some models, we have realised that it is required convert the baseline level of blood pressure to numeric.

```{r}
# Systolic blood pressure
sys.data <- sys.data %>%
  mutate(premean = ifelse(premean == "126,7", "126.7", premean)) %>%
  mutate(premean = ifelse(premean == "126,9", "126.9", premean)) %>%
  mutate(premean = as.numeric(premean))

# removing WBV study from the quantitative synthesis, and recoding interventions to ease model convergence 
sys.data <- sys.data %>%
  mutate(trt = ifelse(trt == "Aerobic + Resistance + Balance exercises", "Aerobic + Resistance", trt)) %>% 
  filter(!studyID == "Dominguez-Muñoz, 2020")

# Diastolic blood pressure
dias.data <- dias.data %>%
  mutate(premean = ifelse(premean == "71,1", "71.1", premean)) %>%
  mutate(premean = ifelse(premean == "72,4", "72.4", premean)) %>%
  mutate(premean = as.numeric(premean))

# Recoding stretching by flexibility
dias.data <- dias.data %>%
  mutate(trt = ifelse(trt == "Stretching", "Flexibility", trt))
```

Neat. Let's move to our first exploratory analyses.

## Systolic blood pressure

First, we are going to conduct an Exploratory Data Analysis aimed to detect potential patterns in the dose-response relationship. In this way, we will be able to decide the best function to model it. Moreover, it is also recommended to observe the distribution of our outcome of interest to ensure that it follows a normal likelihood with posterior meta-analytic purposes.

```{r, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE}
# Distribution of the change from baseline for usual care
sys.data %>%
  filter(trt == "Usual care") %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = y)) +
  stat_halfeye() +
  labs(title = "Distribution of systolic blood pressure responses for usual care",
       x = "Change from baseline (mmHg)",
       y = "Density") +
  theme_minimal()

# Distribution of the change from baseline for physical activity
sys.data %>%
  filter(trt != "Usual care") %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = y)) +
  stat_halfeye() +
  labs(title = "Distribution of systolic blood pressure responses for physical activity",
       x = "Change from baseline (mmHg)",
       y = "Density") +
  theme_minimal()
```

Both responses could be considered normally distributed.

Let's plot the applied dose of physical activity (i.e., weekly energy expenditure) and the changr from baseline to observe potential dose-response relationship forms.

```{r}
if (!all(c("weekly_dose", "y") %in% names(dias.data))) {

}

library(ggplot2)

grid.arrange(lin.plot, l.plot, n2.plot, n3.plot, nrow = 2)

## Network Meta-Analysis

At this point, we are going to conduct non-adjusted (not adding covariates) and adjusted (adding covariates) fixed-effect and random-effects network meta-analysis (NMA) models to summarise the effectiveness of different modalities of physical activity *vs.* the usual care these participants received. Next, we will compute the **posterior predictive distributions** for effectiveness in a new study, whose range of harmful effects is wider than the mean effect of our meta-analysis. In this way, we will determine which type of physical activity is less likely to present harmful effects in future studies, and consider a trade-off between effectiveness and safety to recommend a specific modality in this population.

#### Setting a new classification of treatments

We are going to recode the treatments to obtain different classes as indicated in the American College of Sports Medicine.

```{r}
sys.data <- sys.data %>%
  mutate(trt.2 = case_when(
    trt %in% c("HIIT", "Mixed aerobic exercises", "Cycling", "Running", "Walking") ~ "Aerobic",
    trt == "Mind-body" ~ "Mind-body",
    trt == "Stretching" ~ "Flexibility",
    trt %in% c("Aerobic + Resistance",
               "Aerobic + Resistance + Balance exercises") ~ "Multicomponent",
    trt == "Usual care" ~ "Usual care",
    trt == "Resistance" ~ "Resistance"
  ))

dias.data <- dias.data %>%
  mutate(trt.2 = case_when(
    trt %in% c("HIIT", "Mixed aerobic exercises", "Cycling", "Running", "Walking") ~ "Aerobic",
    trt == "Mind-body" ~ "Mind-body",
    trt == "Flexibility" ~ "Flexibility",
    trt %in% c("Aerobic + Resistance",
               "Aerobic + Resistance + Balance exercises") ~ "Multicomponent",
    trt == "Usual care" ~ "Usual care",
    trt == "Resistance" ~ "Resistance"
  ))

unique(sys.data$trt.2)
unique(dias.data$trt.2)
```

### Setting up the network for systolic blood pressure

We have data on the mean changes from baseline (`y`), associated standard errors (`se`), and sample size for each study-arm (`sample_size`). Therefore, we are using **arm-based** data (sometimes called an *exact* likelihhod), which is preferred where possible in general (more than contrast-based data).

```{r}
# setting up the network_treatment agent
library(ggpubr)
net1 <- set_agd_arm(sys.data,
                   study = studyID,
                   trt = trt.2,
                   y = y,
                   se = se,
                   sample_size = postn,
                   trt_ref = "Usual care")

# what?
net1

# setting up the network_treatment level 3
net2 <- set_agd_arm(sys.data,
                   study = studyID,
                   trt = trt,
                   y = y,
                   se = se,
                   sample_size = postn,
                   trt_ref = "Usual care")

# what?
net2
```

In the summary of our network we observe that we have a total of 60 studies, and 10 treatments (or types of physical activity). Also, information about the type of outcome is indicated (continuous), the reference treatment (`Usual care`), and that our network fullfils with one of the core principles of NMAs, that is the connectivity of the network. Let's see our network.

We have data on the mean changes from baseline (`y`), associated standard errors (`se`), and sample size for each study-arm (`sample_size`). Therefore, we are using **arm-based** data (sometimes called an *exact* likelihhod), which is preferred where possible in general (more than contrast-based data).

```{r}
# setting up the network_treatment agent
library(ggpubr)
net3 <- set_agd_arm(dias.data,
                   study = studyID,
                   trt = trt.2,

                   se = se,
                   sample_size = postn,
                   trt_ref = "Usual care")

# what?
net3

# setting up the network_treatment level 3
net4 <- set_agd_arm(dias.data,
                   study = studyID,
                   trt = trt,
                   y = y,
                   se = se,
                   sample_size = postn,
                   trt_ref = "Usual care")

# what?
net4
```

In the summary of our network we observe that we have a total of 61 studies, and 11 treatments (or types of physical activity). Also, information about the type of outcome is indicated (continuous), the reference treatment (`Usual care`), and that our network fullfils with one of the core principles of NMAs, that is the connectivity of the network. Let's see our network.

### Meta-analysis models_systolic_agent

We will fit fixed-effect and random-effects models, firstly without any covariates, and then with a meta-regression on the continuous covariate `premean`, which is the baseline systolic blood pressure.

#### Fixed-effect meta-analysis (no covariate)

We start by fitting a standard fixed-effect (FE) model without any covariates. We used informative normal prior distributions for the treatments' effects, and study-specific intercepts. We can examine the range of parameter values implied by these prior distributions.

```{r}
summary(normal(scale = 10))
```

Before the optimal prior information selection, we compared the model fit and associated errors of the mean treatment effects between a model with non-information priors (`normal(scale = 100))`), and the one above, and the last one best fitted our estimates. Let's conduct the model.

```{r}
fit_FE <- nma(net1,
              seed = 26012024,
              trt_effects = "fixed",
              prior_intercept = normal(scale = 10),
              prior_trt = normal(scale = 10))
```

Basic parameter summaries are given below.

```{r, collapse=TRUE}
fit_FE
```

#### Random-effects model (no covariate)

In this model, we used a half-normal prior distribution for the heterogeneity standard deviation $\tau$.

```{r}
summary(half_normal(scale = 5))
```

Let's conduct the model.

```{r}
fit_RE <- nma(net1,
              seed = 17012024,
              trt_effects = "random",
              prior_intercept = normal(scale = 10),
              prior_trt = normal(scale = 10),
              prior_het = half_normal(scale = 5))
```

### Fixed-effect meta-analysis with covariate `premean`

We conducted a FE meta-regression model. The regression formula `~.trt:premean` means that the interaction of baseline blood pressure with treatent will be included. We increase `adapt_delta` to 0.99 to remove a small number of divergent transition errors.

```{r}
fit_FE_reg_agent_sys <- nma(net1,
              seed = 17012024,
              trt_effects = "fixed",
              regression = ~.trt:premean,
              prior_intercept = normal(scale = 10),
              prior_trt = normal(scale = 10),
              prior_reg = normal(scale = 100),
              adapt_delta = 0.99)

fit_FE_reg_agent_sys

```

```{r}
fit_FE_reg_trt_sys <- nma(net2,
              seed = 17012024,
              trt_effects = "fixed",
              regression = ~.trt:premean,
              prior_intercept = normal(scale = 10),
              prior_trt = normal(scale = 10),
              prior_reg = normal(scale = 100),
              adapt_delta = 0.99)

fit_FE_reg_trt_sys
```

```{r}
fit_FE_reg_agent_dias <- nma(net3,
              seed = 17012024,
              trt_effects = "fixed",
              regression = ~.trt:premean,
              prior_intercept = normal(scale = 10),
              prior_trt = normal(scale = 10),
              prior_reg = normal(scale = 100),
              adapt_delta = 0.99)
```

```{r}
fit_FE_reg_trt_dias <- nma(net4,
              seed = 17012024,
              trt_effects = "fixed",
              regression = ~.trt:premean,
              prior_intercept = normal(scale = 10),
              prior_trt = normal(scale = 10),
              prior_reg = normal(scale = 100),
              adapt_delta = 0.99)
```

#### Random-effects meta-analysis with covariate `premean`
### Fixed-effect meta-analysis with covariate `premean`

We conducted a FE meta-regression model. The regression formula `~.trt:premean` means that the interaction of baseline blood pressure with treatent will be included. We increase `adapt_delta` to 0.99 to remove a small number of divergent transition errors.

```{r}
fit_RE_reg_agent_sys <- nma(net1,
              seed = 17012024,
              trt_effects = "random",
              regression = ~.trt:premean,
              prior_intercept = normal(scale = 10),
              prior_trt = normal(scale = 10),
              prior_reg = normal(scale = 100),
              adapt_delta = 0.99)
```

```{r}
fit_RE_reg_trt_sys <- nma(net2,
              seed = 17012024,
              trt_effects = "random",
              regression = ~.trt:premean,
              prior_intercept = normal(scale = 10),
              prior_trt = normal(scale = 10),
              prior_reg = normal(scale = 100),
              adapt_delta = 0.99)
```

```{r}
fit_RE_reg_agent_dias <- nma(net3,
              seed = 17012024,
              trt_effects = "random",
              regression = ~.trt:premean,
              prior_intercept = normal(scale = 10),
              prior_trt = normal(scale = 10),
              prior_reg = normal(scale = 100),
              adapt_delta = 0.99)
```

```{r}
fit_RE_reg_trt_dias <- nma(net4,
              seed = 17012024,
              trt_effects = "random",
              regression = ~.trt:premean,
              prior_intercept = normal(scale = 10),
              prior_trt = normal(scale = 10),
              prior_reg = normal(scale = 100),
              adapt_delta = 0.99)
```
#### Model fit and comparison

Model fit was checked comparing the residual deviance (on 147 data points), the number of parameters, and the Deviance Information Criterion (DIC).

```{r, collapse=TRUE}
# fixed-effect (no covariate)
(dic_FE <- dic(fit_FE))

# random-effects (no covariate)
(dic_RE <- dic(fit_RE))

# fixed-effect with covariate
(dic_FE_cov <- dic(fit_FE_reg_agent_sys))

# random-effects with covariate
(dic_RE_cov <- dic(fit_RE_reg_agent_sys))

```

We might prefer the models with the baseline blood pressure as covariate due to the use of change from baseline scores as our main outcome, and the need of controlling them by baseline values. Based on methodological evidence, those models are also known as *ANCOVA* models, which give us greater statistical power. Moreover, between fixed-effect and random-effects model, we selected the **fixed-effect** model based on **parsimony**, since there are no huge differences between DIC values. In addition, the introduction of the intensity of the activity did not improve the fit of the model. This artifact could be cause by the fact that most of specific activities are associated with fixed intensities.

We can observe the $\beta$ regression coefficients for the treatments below.

```{r}
plot(fit_FE_reg,
     pars = "beta",
     ref_line = 0,
     stat = "halfeye")
```

In addition, we can inspect the residual deviance contributions for each data point to detect those that did not fit as well as expected.

```{r, fig.width=15, fig.height=7}
plot(dic_FE_cov)
```

#### Checking for inconsistency

We first fit an unrelated mean effects (UME) model to assess the consistency assumption in NMAs.

```{r}
fit_inc <- nma(net,
              seed = 17012024,
              trt_effects = "fixed",
              regression = ~.trt:premean,
              prior_intercept = normal(scale = 10),
              prior_trt = normal(scale = 10),
              prior_reg = normal(scale = 100),
              adapt_delta = 0.99,
              consistency = "ume")
```

Next, we compare the model fit statistics of both models (*consistent* and UME).

```{r, collapse=TRUE}
# consistent model
dic_FE_cov

# UME model
(dic_FE_inc <-  dic(fit_inc))
```

We see that our consistent model better fits the data. However, it is also important to examine the individual contributions to model fit of each data point under the two models (a so-called *dev-dev plot*).

```{r, echo=FALSE, fig.height=6, fig.width=6}
tiff("dev_dev_trt.tiff", height = 6, width = 6, res = 1200, units = "in")
plot(dic_FE_cov, dic_FE_inc, show_uncertainty = FALSE)
dev.off()
```

All points lie roughly on the line of equality, though there are some that lie on the UME model quadrant, reflecting worse fit. Thus, there is no evidence for inconsistency.

### Relative effects

We can produce estimates of the relative effect of different physical activity modalities in people with T2DM at any baseline blood pressure level.

```{r, collapse=TRUE}
# systolic blood pressure_agent
(rel_effect_agent_sys <- relative_effects(fit_RE_reg_agent_sys,
                                newdata = tibble::tibble(premean = seq(125, 145, 10)),
                                study = paste(premean, "mmHg")))
# systolic blood pressure_trt
(rel_effect_trt_sys <- relative_effects(fit_FE_reg_trt_sys,
                                newdata = tibble::tibble(premean = seq(125, 145, 10)),
                                study = paste(premean, "mmHg")))
# diastolic blood pressure_agent
(rel_effect_agent_dias <- relative_effects(fit_FE_reg_agent_dias,
                                newdata = tibble::tibble(premean = c(75, 85, 90)),
                                study = paste(premean, "mmHg")))

# diastolic blood pressure_trt
(rel_effect_trt_dias <- relative_effects(fit_FE_reg_trt_dias,
                                newdata = tibble::tibble(premean = c(75, 85, 90)),
                                study = paste(premean, "mmHg")))
```

Next, we plot these estimates.

```{r, fig.height=15, fig.width=8, echo=FALSE}
tiff("rel_eff_agent_sys.tiff", height = 7, width = 7, units = "in", res = 300)
plot(rel_effect_agent_sys, ref_line = 0, stat = "halfeye") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(-100, 100, 10))
dev.off()
```

```{r, fig.height=15, fig.width=8, echo=FALSE}
tiff("rel_eff_trt_sys.tiff", height = 7, width = 7, units = "in", res = 300)
plot(rel_effect_trt_sys, ref_line = 0, stat = "halfeye") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(-100, 100, 10))
dev.off()
```

```{r, fig.height=15, fig.width=8, echo=FALSE}
tiff("rel_eff_agent_dias.tiff", height = 7, width = 7, units = "in", res = 300)
plot(rel_effect_agent_dias, ref_line = 0, stat = "halfeye") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(-100, 100, 10))
dev.off()
```

```{r, fig.height=15, fig.width=8, echo=FALSE}
tiff("rel_eff_trt_dias.tiff", height = 7, width = 7, units = "in", res = 1200)
plot(rel_effect_trt_dias, ref_line = 0, stat = "halfeye") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(-100, 100, 10))
dev.off()
```

**Aerobic physical activity** was the unique intervention that achieved a statistically significant reduction of 3.77 $mmHg$ (95% CrI -5.92 to -1.63) on the systolic blood pressure of people with T2DM and elevated blood pressure (130 mmHg). For participants with a more severe hypertension stage, aerobic phyical activity achieved blood pressure reductions considered as clinically meaningful: -6.95 $mmHg$ (95% CrI -10.94 to -3.02) on hypertension stage 1 (140 $mmHg$), and -10.13 $mmHg$ (95% CrI -18.28 to -1.98) on hypertension stage 2 (150 $mmHg$). Interestingly, **mind-body training** showed potential benefits for people with stage 1 hypertension (MCFB = -13.73; 95% CrI -27.15 to 0.00).

The unique intervention that achieved a statistically significant effect on participants with a baseline SBP of 130 $mmHg$ was **High Intensity Interval Training (HIIT)** (MCFB = -2.96; 95% CrI -5.60 to -0.29). The same happened for **HIIT** in participants with a baseline of 135 $mmHg$ (MCFB = -5.78; 95% CrI -9.19 to -2.30), and 140 $mmHg$ (MCFB = -8.60; 95% CrI -15.92 to -1.46). However, it is important to highlight that these effects could be considered as **clinically** meaningful reductions on SBP (i.e., between 5 to 10 $mmHg$ compared with baseline). Finally, for people with hypertension stage 2 (i.e., SBP greater than 140 $mmHg$), **mind-body training** (MCFB = -13.75; 95% CrI -27.42 to -0.54) and **HIIT** (MCFB = -11.42; 95% CrI -22.93 to -0.11) also achieved clinically important differences on SBP. From this baseline level, the heterogeneity on the effects is substantial.

####sophisticated plot

###### *Agent-level_systolic*

```{r}
# create range of baseline blood pressure levels
lat.range <- range(sys.data$premean)

# create tibble with 1-unit increase on blood pressure
lat.dat <- tibble(premean = seq(lat.range[1], lat.range[2], 1))

# data wrangling for fitting the plot

                  study = paste(premean, "mmHg"))

# Paso 2: Obtener efectos relativos a partir del modelo ajustado

  fit_FE_reg_agent_sys,
  newdata = lat.dat,
  study = lat.dat$study
)

# Paso 3: Expandir trt labels para mergearlos con predicciones

# Paso 4: Unir todo

  bind_cols(lat.dat_expanded, trts)

# Paso 5: Preparar base de datos con tamaños muestrales

  group_by(studyID) %>%
  mutate(sample_size = sum(postn)) %>%
  ungroup()

# Paso 6: Gráfico final

  ggplot(aes(x = premean)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, col = "grey60") +

  facet_wrap(~trts, scales = "free") +
  labs(x = "Baseline systolic blood pressure",

  scale_size("Sample size") +
  theme_multinma() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom") +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = seq(-100, 100, 10))

dev.off()

### Treatment rankings at agent level

We computed posterior treatment rankings from meta-regression models to obtain a ranking by study population (i.e., different baseline systolic blood pressure levels).

```{r, fig.height=12, fig.width=8, collapse=TRUE}
# treatment rankings agent sys
(rank_agent_sys <- posterior_ranks(fit_FE_reg_agent_sys, 
                         lower_better = TRUE, 
                         newdata = tibble(premean = c(125, 135, 145)),
                         study = paste(premean, "mmHg")))

# plot sys agent
tiff("rank_sys_agent.tiff", height = 7, width = 7, units = "in", res = 300)
plot(rank_agent_sys)
dev.off()

# treatment rankings agent dias
(rank_agent_dias <- posterior_ranks(fit_FE_reg_agent_dias, 
                         lower_better = TRUE, 
                         newdata = tibble(premean = c(75, 85, 90)),
                         study = paste(premean, "mmHg")))

# plot dias agent
tiff("rank_dias_agent.tiff", height = 7, width = 7, units = "in", res = 300)
plot(rank_agent_dias)
dev.off()
```

**Aerobic physical activities** was the best ranked intervention for people with elevated blood pressure. However, for people diagnosed with stages 1 and 2 of hypertension, mind-body activities were the most recommended type of intervention.

##### *Ranking at treatment-level*

```{r, fig.height=12, fig.width=8, collapse=TRUE}
# treatment rankings trt sys
(rank_trt_sys <- posterior_ranks(fit_FE_reg_trt_sys, 
                         lower_better = TRUE, 
                         newdata = tibble(premean = c(125, 135, 145)),
                         study = paste(premean, "mmHg")))

# plot sys trt
tiff("rank_sys_trt.tiff", height = 7, width = 7, units = "in", res = 300)
plot(rank_trt_sys)
dev.off()

# treatment rankings agent dias
(rank_trt_dias <- posterior_ranks(fit_FE_reg_trt_dias, 
                         lower_better = TRUE, 
                         newdata = tibble(premean = c(75, 85, 90)),
                         study = paste(premean, "mmHg")))

# plot dias agent
tiff("rank_dias_trt.tiff", height = 7, width = 7, units = "in", res = 300)
plot(rank_trt_dias)
dev.off()
```

At lower baseline SBP levels (below 130 $mmHg$; i.e., normal or elevated SBP), the modalities of **cycling**, **resistance exercises**, and **walking** seem to be the most effective interventions. Above this value (for hypertension stages 1 and 2), the modalities that had associated greatest SBP reductions were **mind-body training**, **HIIT**, and **mixed aerobic exercises**, since **running** presented large relative effects heterogeneity.

#### OV-Dose Response OVERALL

##### Estadistico - Dosis Systolic blood pressure

```{r}
# 🔍 Modelo lineal simple
lm_simple <- lm(y ~ weekly_dose, data = sys.data)
summary(lm_simple)  # Revisa el valor-p del coeficiente de weekly_dose

# 📈 Modelo con spline natural (2 grados de libertad)
lm_spline2 <- lm(y ~ ns(weekly_dose, 2), data = sys.data)

# 📊 Comparación de modelos: lineal vs spline
anova(lm_simple, lm_spline2)

# 📦 Modelo con spline más flexible (3 grados de libertad)
lm_spline3 <- lm(y ~ ns(weekly_dose, 3), data = sys.data)

# 📊 Comparación lineal vs spline 3
anova(lm_simple, lm_spline3)

# ✅ Evaluación del modelo categórico
# Clasificamos dosis en 4 grupos (personalizable)
sys.data$dose_group <- cut(
  sys.data$weekly_dose,
  breaks = c(-Inf, 0, 500, 1000, Inf),
  labels = c("Usual Care", "Low", "Medium", "High")
)

# Modelo categórico (ANOVA)
lm_cat <- aov(y ~ dose_group, data = sys.data)
summary(lm_cat)

# Comparaciones múltiples entre grupos
TukeyHSD(lm_cat)

```

Existe una relación dosis-respuesta estadísticamente significativa entre la actividad física semanal y la reducción de presión sistólica en el análisis global (overall).

Los modelos con splines mejoran la explicación, revelando una posible forma no lineal, mientras que los análisis categóricos sugieren que el beneficio clínico se concentra en alcanzar un umbral mínimo de actividad física, sin ganancias adicionales sustanciales en dosis más altas.

Los splines explican mejor la variabilidad que el modelo lineal simple (ambos p \< 0.001).

El modelo con 2 o 3 df es mejor que el lineal.

No hay una mejora marcada de 3 df sobre 2 df (F de mejora es leve), por tanto, ns(x, 2) podría ser preferible si se busca parsimonia.

##### Dosis Óptima Systolic blood pressure

```{r}

# Preprocesamiento
sys.data_valido <- sys.data %>%
  filter(!is.na(y), !is.na(weekly_dose))

# Modelo robusto
ajustar_spline_seguro <- function(data) {
  modelo <- lm(y ~ ns(weekly_dose, 3), data = data)
  if (qr(model.matrix(modelo))$rank < ncol(model.matrix(modelo))) {
    message("⚠️ Spline(3) no viable, usando spline(2)")
    modelo <- lm(y ~ ns(weekly_dose, 2), data = data)
  }
  return(modelo)
}

lm_spline <- ajustar_spline_seguro(sys.data_valido)

# Predicciones
doses <- seq(min(sys.data_valido$weekly_dose), max(sys.data_valido$weekly_dose), length.out = 1000)
pred_df <- data.frame(weekly_dose = doses)
pred_df$predicted <- predict(lm_spline, newdata = pred_df)

# Dosis óptima
optimal_index <- which.min(pred_df$predicted)
optimal_dose <- pred_df$weekly_dose[optimal_index]
optimal_response <- pred_df$predicted[optimal_index]

# Resultados
cat("📍 Dosis óptima estimada:", round(optimal_dose, 1), "MET-min/semana\n")
cat("🩺 Cambio estimado en presión sistólica:", round(optimal_response, 2), "mmHg\n")

# Gráfico limpio y robusto
ggplot(sys.data_valido, aes(x = weekly_dose, y = y)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_line(data = pred_df, aes(x = weekly_dose, y = predicted), color = "blue", size = 1) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = optimal_dose, linetype = "dashed", color = "red") +
  annotate("text", x = optimal_dose, y = min(pred_df$predicted),
           label = paste0("Dosis óptima:\n", round(optimal_dose, 0), " MET-min/sem"),
           hjust = -0.1, color = "red") +
  labs(
    x = "Dosis semanal (MET-min)",
    y = "Cambio en presión sistólica (mmHg)",
    title = "Curva dosis-respuesta con dosis óptima (modelo externo)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

```


##### Dosis minima, maxima y optima Systolic blood pressure

```{r}

library(ggplot2)
library(splines)
library(dplyr)

# ⚙️ Paso 1: Validar y limpiar datos
sys.data_valido <- sys.data %>%
  filter(!is.na(y), !is.na(weekly_dose))

# ⚙️ Paso 2: Modelo spline robusto
ajustar_spline_seguro <- function(data) {
  modelo <- lm(y ~ ns(weekly_dose, 3), data = data)
  if (qr(model.matrix(modelo))$rank < ncol(model.matrix(modelo))) {
    message("⚠️ Modelo spline(3) rank-deficient, usando spline(2)")
    modelo <- lm(y ~ ns(weekly_dose, 2), data = data)
  }
  return(modelo)
}

lm_spline <- ajustar_spline_seguro(sys.data_valido)

# 📈 Paso 3: Curva predicha + IC
doses <- seq(min(sys.data_valido$weekly_dose), max(sys.data_valido$weekly_dose), length.out = 1000)
pred_data <- data.frame(weekly_dose = doses)
preds <- predict(lm_spline, newdata = pred_data, interval = "confidence")
pred_curve <- cbind(pred_data, preds)

# 📍 Paso 4: Dosis óptima
opt_index <- which.min(pred_curve$fit)
dose_optimal <- pred_curve$weekly_dose[opt_index]
y_optimal <- pred_curve$fit[opt_index]

# 🟦 Paso 5: Zona OMS
shade_min <- 600
shade_max <- 1200

# 🖼️ Paso 6: Graficar con robustez
tiff("Curva_Dosis_Con_Optima_Sistolica.tiff", width = 9, height = 6, units = "in", res = 300)


# Si no lo has hecho antes, define el rango del eje Y si lo necesitas
y_min <- min(pred_curve$lwr)
y_max <- max(pred_curve$upr)

ggplot() +
  # Área sombreada de recomendaciones de la OMS
  geom_rect(
    aes(xmin = shade_min, xmax = shade_max, ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf),
    fill = "gray70", alpha = 0.2
  ) +

  # Curva de predicción en negro
  geom_line(
    data = pred_curve,
    aes(x = weekly_dose, y = fit),
    color = "black", size = 1
  ) +
  
  # Intervalos de confianza (líneas punteadas)
  geom_line(
    data = pred_curve,
    aes(x = weekly_dose, y = lwr),
    linetype = "dashed", color = "black"
  ) +
  geom_line(
    data = pred_curve,
    aes(x = weekly_dose, y = upr),
    linetype = "dashed", color = "black"
  ) +

  # Línea roja corta centrada en el punto óptimo
  geom_segment(
    aes(
      x = dose_optimal, xend = dose_optimal,
      y = y_optimal - 0.0,
      yend = y_optimal + 5.0
    ),
    color = "red", linewidth = 0.8
  ) +

  # Punto rojo en la dosis óptima
  geom_point(
    aes(x = dose_optimal, y = y_optimal),
    color = "red", size = 3
  ) +

  # Texto vertical cerca del punto rojo
  annotate(
    "text",
    x = dose_optimal + 15,
    y = y_optimal + 2.5,
    label = paste0("MCID at ", round(dose_optimal), " METs-min/week"),
    angle = 90, hjust = 0.3, vjust = 0.9,
    color = "red", size = 3.4
  ) +

  # Texto centrado en el área gris
  annotate(
    "text",
    x = (shade_min + shade_max) / 2,
    y = max(pred_curve$fit) + 1.7,
    label = "WHO PA recommendations",
    size = 4.5
  ) +
  
  # Ejes
  labs(
    x = "Physical activity dose (METs-min/week)",
    y = "Estimated change in systolic blood pressure (Δ mmHg)"
  ) +

  # Tema y tipografía
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    text = element_text(family = "Arial"),
    plot.title = element_text(size = 14, face = "bold")
  )


```

#### AG-Dose Response Agent level

##### Estadistico - Dosis Systolic blood pressure at agent level

```{r}

# Filtrar agentes válidos
sys.data_activos <- sys.data[!sys.data$trt.2 %in% c("Usual care", "Flexibility"), ]

# Agrupar por agente
agente_split <- split(sys.data_activos, sys.data_activos$trt.2)

# Loop para mostrar salida como en OVERALL
for (nombre_agente in names(agente_split)) {
  datos <- agente_split[[nombre_agente]]
  
  if (nrow(datos) < 5 || length(unique(datos$weekly_dose)) < 4) {
    cat("\n⛔ Agente:", nombre_agente, "- Insuficiente variación\n")
    next
  }
  
  cat("\n==============================")
  cat("\n📊 Agente:", nombre_agente, "\n")
  cat("==============================\n")
  
  modelo_lin <- lm(y ~ weekly_dose, data = datos)
  modelo_ns2 <- lm(y ~ ns(weekly_dose, 2), data = datos)
  modelo_ns3 <- lm(y ~ ns(weekly_dose, 3), data = datos)
  
  cat("\n🔹 Modelo Lineal:\n")
  print(summary(modelo_lin))
  
  cat("\n🔸 ANOVA: Lineal vs Spline (2 df):\n")
  print(anova(modelo_lin, modelo_ns2))
  
  cat("\n🔸 ANOVA: Lineal vs Spline (3 df):\n")
  print(anova(modelo_lin, modelo_ns3))
}

# Filtrar agentes válidos
sys.data_activos <- sys.data[!sys.data$trt.2 %in% c("Usual care", "Flexibility"), ]

# Agrupar por agente
agente_split <- split(sys.data_activos, sys.data_activos$trt.2)

# Loop por agente para mostrar resultados
for (nombre_agente in names(agente_split)) {
  datos <- agente_split[[nombre_agente]]
  
  if (nrow(datos) < 5 || length(unique(datos$weekly_dose)) < 4) {
    cat("\n⛔ Agente:", nombre_agente, "- Insuficiente variación\n")
    next
  }
  
  cat("\n\n======================================")
  cat("\n📊 Análisis de agente:", nombre_agente)
  cat("\n======================================\n")
  
  # 📌 Modelo lineal simple
  modelo_lin <- lm(y ~ weekly_dose, data = datos)
  cat("\n🔹 Modelo Lineal:\n")
  print(summary(modelo_lin))
  
  # 📈 Comparación con spline (2 df)
  modelo_ns2 <- lm(y ~ ns(weekly_dose, 2), data = datos)
  cat("\n🔸 ANOVA: Lineal vs Spline (2 df):\n")
  print(anova(modelo_lin, modelo_ns2))
  
  # 📈 Comparación con spline (3 df)
  modelo_ns3 <- lm(y ~ ns(weekly_dose, 3), data = datos)
  cat("\n🔸 ANOVA: Lineal vs Spline (3 df):\n")
  print(anova(modelo_lin, modelo_ns3))
  
  # ✅ Clasificación por grupos de dosis
  datos$dose_group <- cut(
    datos$weekly_dose,
    breaks = c(-Inf, 0, 500, 1000, Inf),
    labels = c("Usual Care", "Low", "Medium", "High")
  )
  
  # ⚠️ Evitar errores por grupos vacíos
  if (length(unique(na.omit(datos$dose_group))) < 2) {
    cat("\n⚠️ No se puede realizar ANOVA categórica (grupos insuficientes)\n")
    next
  }
  
  # 📊 ANOVA categórico
  modelo_cat <- aov(y ~ dose_group, data = datos)
  cat("\n✅ ANOVA por grupo de dosis (categorías):\n")
  print(summary(modelo_cat))
  
  # 🧪 Comparaciones múltiples
  cat("\n🔍 Comparaciones múltiples (Tukey HSD):\n")
  print(TukeyHSD(modelo_cat))
}


```

Ninguno de los agentes (Aerobic, Mind-body, Multicomponent, Resistance) muestra una relación dosis-respuesta estadísticamente significativa en presión sistólica, ni bajo modelos lineales, ni spline, ni por categorías.

Explorando los agent level por cada categoria del baseline tampoco aparecen dosis significativa. Solo en Excepción leve para Aerobic – Alta presión inicial:
Tiene una dosis óptima estimada de 422.4 MET-min y una caída de −9.59 mmHg. Su R² ajustado es 0.832 → si ese valor está bien calculado, podría ser una excepción.
Pero no hemos visto los p-valores para ese modelo concreto estratificado por nivel basal, así que no podemos concluir significancia aún sin el modelo completo para esa subpoblación.

###### Dosis Óptima Systolic blood pressure agent level
Se deja aqui pero al no salir nada significativo en los estadisticos, no merece la pena calcular unos datos y presentarlos. Igualmente dejamos el código para adaptarlo a otros metaánalisis
```{r}
# Filtrar solo agentes activos
sys.data_agente <- sys.data %>%
  filter(!trt.2 %in% c("Usual care", "Flexibility"))

# Dividir datos por agente
split_agente <- split(sys.data_agente, sys.data_agente$trt.2)

# Función para calcular dosis óptima y graficar
optima_agente <- map(split_agente, function(datos) {
  if (nrow(datos) < 5 || length(unique(datos$weekly_dose)) < 4) return(NULL)

  modelo <- lm(y ~ ns(weekly_dose, 3), data = datos)
  
  dosis_seq <- seq(min(datos$weekly_dose), max(datos$weekly_dose), length.out = 1000)
  predicciones <- predict(modelo, newdata = data.frame(weekly_dose = dosis_seq))
  
  opt_index <- which.min(predicciones)
  opt_dose <- dosis_seq[opt_index]
  opt_resp <- predicciones[opt_index]
  
  grafico <- ggplot(datos, aes(x = weekly_dose, y = y)) +
    geom_point(alpha = 0.5) +
    stat_smooth(method = "lm", formula = y ~ ns(x, 3), col = "blue", se = FALSE) +
    geom_vline(xintercept = opt_dose, linetype = "dashed", color = "red") +
    annotate("text", x = opt_dose, y = min(predicciones),
             label = paste0(round(opt_dose, 0), " MET-min/sem"),
             hjust = -0.1, color = "red") +
    labs(title = paste("Dosis óptima -", unique(datos$trt.2)),
         x = "Dosis semanal (MET-min)", y = "Cambio en presión sistólica (mmHg)") +
    theme_minimal()
  
  list(
    agente = unique(datos$trt.2),
    dosis_optima = round(opt_dose, 1),
    cambio_estimado = round(opt_resp, 2),
    grafico = grafico
  )
})

# Filtrar resultados válidos
optima_agente <- compact(optima_agente)

# Imprimir resumen de dosis óptimas
map_dfr(optima_agente, ~tibble(
  agente = .x$agente,
  dosis_optima = .x$dosis_optima,
  cambio_estimado = .x$cambio_estimado
))

# Por ejemplo, para ver la de Aerobic
optima_agente[["Aerobic"]]$grafico

# O para recorrerlas todas:
walk(optima_agente, ~print(.x$grafico))


```

###### Dosis minima, maxima y optima Systolic blood pressure at agent level
Se deja aqui pero al no salir nada significativo en los estadisticos, no merece la pena calcular unos datos y presentarlos. Igualmente dejamos el código para adaptarlo a otros metaánalisis
```{r}
library(ggplot2)
library(splines)
library(dplyr)
library(purrr)

# Definir zona recomendada por la OMS
shade_min <- 600
shade_max <- 1200

# Filtrar solo agentes activos (excluyendo Usual care y Flexibility)
sys.data_agente <- sys.data %>% 
  filter(!trt.2 %in% c("Usual care", "Flexibility"))

# Separar por agente
split_agente <- split(sys.data_agente, sys.data_agente$trt.2)

# Función para generar gráfico con curva spline, IC y zona OMS
grafico_dosis_agente <- map(split_agente, function(df) {
  if (nrow(df) < 5 || length(unique(df$weekly_dose)) < 4) return(NULL)
  
  modelo <- lm(y ~ ns(weekly_dose, 3), data = df)
  
  dosis_seq <- seq(min(df$weekly_dose), max(df$weekly_dose), length.out = 1000)
  pred_data <- data.frame(weekly_dose = dosis_seq)
  preds <- predict(modelo, newdata = pred_data, interval = "confidence")
  pred_curve <- cbind(pred_data, preds)
  
  opt_index <- which.min(pred_curve$fit)
  dose_opt <- pred_curve$weekly_dose[opt_index]
  y_opt <- pred_curve$fit[opt_index]
  
  g <- ggplot() +
    geom_rect(aes(xmin = shade_min, xmax = shade_max, ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf),
              fill = "gray70", alpha = 0.2) +
    geom_line(data = pred_curve, aes(x = weekly_dose, y = fit), size = 1) +
    geom_line(data = pred_curve, aes(x = weekly_dose, y = lwr), linetype = "dashed") +
    geom_line(data = pred_curve, aes(x = weekly_dose, y = upr), linetype = "dashed") +
    geom_vline(xintercept = dose_opt, linetype = "dashed", color = "red", linewidth = 0.8) +
    annotate("text", x = dose_opt, y = y_opt,
             label = paste0("Optimal ≈ ", round(dose_opt, 0), " MET-min"),
             vjust = -0.7, hjust = -0.05, color = "red", size = 4) +
    annotate("text", x = (shade_min + shade_max)/2, y = max(pred_curve$fit),
             label = "WHO PA recommendations", vjust = -0.5, size = 4) +
    annotate("text", x = 0, y = min(pred_curve$lwr),
             label = "Model fit:\nSpline (3 df)", hjust = 0, vjust = 0, fontface = "bold") +
    labs(
      title = paste("Dose-response by agent:", unique(df$trt.2)),
      x = "Dose of physical activity (METs-min/week)",
      y = "Estimated effect (Δ systolic BP)"
    ) +
    theme_minimal()
  
  list(
    agente = unique(df$trt.2),
    dosis_optima = round(dose_opt, 1),
    efecto_optimo = round(y_opt, 2),
    grafico = g
  )
})

# Limpiar nulos
grafico_dosis_agente <- compact(grafico_dosis_agente)

# Mostrar tabla resumen
map_dfr(grafico_dosis_agente, ~ tibble(
  agente = .x$agente,
  dosis_optima = .x$dosis_optima,
  cambio_estimado = .x$efecto_optimo
))


# Ver un gráfico específico (por ejemplo, Aerobic)
grafico_dosis_agente[["Aerobic"]]$grafico

# Mostrar todos
walk(grafico_dosis_agente, ~print(.x$grafico))


```

Cycling muestra una posible dosis óptima significativa en presión sistólica, según el modelo spline.

##### Estadistico - Dosis Diastolic blood pressure

```{r}
# 📦 Paquetes necesarios

# 🔍 Modelo lineal simple
lm_simple_dias <- lm(y ~ weekly_dose, data = dias.data)
summary(lm_simple_dias)  # Revisa el valor-p del coeficiente de weekly_dose

# 📈 Modelo con spline natural (2 grados de libertad)
lm_spline2_dias <- lm(y ~ ns(weekly_dose, 2), data = dias.data)

# 📊 Comparación de modelos: lineal vs spline 2
anova(lm_simple_dias, lm_spline2_dias)

# 📈 Modelo con spline más flexible (3 grados de libertad)
lm_spline3_dias <- lm(y ~ ns(weekly_dose, 3), data = dias.data)

# 📊 Comparación de modelos: lineal vs spline 3
anova(lm_simple_dias, lm_spline3_dias)

# ✅ Evaluación del modelo categórico
# Clasificamos dosis en 4 grupos (ajustable)
dias.data$dose_group <- cut(
  dias.data$weekly_dose,
  breaks = c(-Inf, 0, 500, 1000, Inf),
  labels = c("Usual Care", "Low", "Medium", "High")
)

# Modelo categórico (ANOVA)
lm_cat_dias <- aov(y ~ dose_group, data = dias.data)
summary(lm_cat_dias)

# Comparaciones múltiples entre grupos
TukeyHSD(lm_cat_dias)

```
 la relación dosis-respuesta para presión diastólica es estadísticamente significativa en todos los enfoques: lineal, spline y categórico.
 
En este caso, el modelo con spline(3 df) es el mejor para el modelo, porque:

Mejora significativamente respecto al modelo lineal.

Permite representar curvaturas complejas, necesarias para detectar una dosis mínima eficaz o dosis óptima.

##### Dosis Óptima Diastolic blood pressure overall level

```{r}

library(ggplot2)
library(splines)
library(dplyr)

# 📦 Preprocesamiento
dias.data_valido <- dias.data %>%
  filter(!is.na(y), !is.na(weekly_dose))

# 🧠 Función robusta para ajustar el modelo spline
ajustar_spline_seguro <- function(data) {
  modelo <- lm(y ~ ns(weekly_dose, 3), data = data)
  if (qr(model.matrix(modelo))$rank < ncol(model.matrix(modelo))) {
    message("⚠️ Spline(3) no viable, usando spline(2)")
    modelo <- lm(y ~ ns(weekly_dose, 2), data = data)
  }
  return(modelo)
}

# ⚙️ Ajustar el modelo
lm_spline_dias <- ajustar_spline_seguro(dias.data_valido)

# 🔮 Predicciones
doses_dias <- seq(min(dias.data_valido$weekly_dose), 
                  max(dias.data_valido$weekly_dose), 
                  length.out = 1000)
pred_df_dias <- data.frame(weekly_dose = doses_dias)
pred_df_dias$predicted <- predict(lm_spline_dias, newdata = pred_df_dias)

# 🎯 Dosis óptima
optimal_index_dias <- which.min(pred_df_dias$predicted)
optimal_dose_dias <- pred_df_dias$weekly_dose[optimal_index_dias]
optimal_response_dias <- pred_df_dias$predicted[optimal_index_dias]

# 📢 Resultados
cat("📍 Dosis óptima estimada:", round(optimal_dose_dias, 1), "MET-min/semana\n")
cat("🩺 Cambio estimado en presión diastólica:", round(optimal_response_dias, 2), "mmHg\n")

# 📊 Gráfico final
ggplot(dias.data_valido, aes(x = weekly_dose, y = y)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_line(data = pred_df_dias, aes(x = weekly_dose, y = predicted), color = "blue", size = 1) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = optimal_dose_dias, linetype = "dashed", color = "red") +
  annotate("text", x = optimal_dose_dias, y = min(pred_df_dias$predicted),
           label = paste0("Dosis óptima:\n", round(optimal_dose_dias, 0), " MET-min/sem"),
           hjust = -0.1, color = "red") +
  labs(
    x = "Dosis semanal (MET-min)",
    y = "Cambio en presión diastólica (mmHg)",
    title = "Curva dosis-respuesta con dosis óptima (modelo externo)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

```
Spline(3) no viable, usando spline(2)

##### Dosis minima, maxima y optima diastolic blood pressure overall

```{r}

library(ggplot2)
library(splines)
library(dplyr)

# ⚙️ Paso 1: Validar y limpiar datos
dias.data_valido <- dias.data %>%
  filter(!is.na(y), !is.na(weekly_dose))

# ⚙️ Paso 2: Modelo spline robusto
ajustar_spline_seguro <- function(data) {
  modelo <- lm(y ~ ns(weekly_dose, 3), data = data)
  if (qr(model.matrix(modelo))$rank < ncol(model.matrix(modelo))) {
    message("⚠️ Modelo spline(3) rank-deficient, usando spline(2)")
    modelo <- lm(y ~ ns(weekly_dose, 2), data = data)
  }
  return(modelo)
}

lm_spline <- ajustar_spline_seguro(dias.data_valido)

# 📈 Paso 3: Curva predicha + IC
doses <- seq(min(dias.data_valido$weekly_dose), max(dias.data_valido$weekly_dose), length.out = 1000)
pred_data <- data.frame(weekly_dose = doses)
preds <- predict(lm_spline, newdata = pred_data, interval = "confidence")
pred_curve <- cbind(pred_data, preds)

# 📍 Paso 4: Dosis óptima
opt_index <- which.min(pred_curve$fit)
dose_optimal <- pred_curve$weekly_dose[opt_index]
y_optimal <- pred_curve$fit[opt_index]

# 🟦 Paso 5: Zona OMS
shade_min <- 600
shade_max <- 1200

# 🖼️ Paso 6: Graficar con robustez
tiff("Curva_Dosis_Con_Optima_Diastolica.tiff", width = 9, height = 6, units = "in", res = 300)


# Si no lo has hecho antes, define el rango del eje Y si lo necesitas
y_min <- min(pred_curve$lwr)
y_max <- max(pred_curve$upr)

ggplot() +
  # Área sombreada de recomendaciones de la OMS
  geom_rect(
    aes(xmin = shade_min, xmax = shade_max, ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf),
    fill = "gray70", alpha = 0.2
  ) +

  # Curva de predicción en negro
  geom_line(
    data = pred_curve,
    aes(x = weekly_dose, y = fit),
    color = "black", size = 1
  ) +
  
  # Intervalos de confianza (líneas punteadas)
  geom_line(
    data = pred_curve,
    aes(x = weekly_dose, y = lwr),
    linetype = "dashed", color = "black"
  ) +
  geom_line(
    data = pred_curve,
    aes(x = weekly_dose, y = upr),
    linetype = "dashed", color = "black"
  ) +

  # Línea roja corta centrada en el punto óptimo
  geom_segment(
    aes(
      x = dose_optimal, xend = dose_optimal,
      y = y_optimal - 0.0,
      yend = y_optimal + 3.7
    ),
    color = "red", linewidth = 0.8
  ) +

  # Punto rojo en la dosis óptima
  geom_point(
    aes(x = dose_optimal, y = y_optimal),
    color = "red", size = 3
  ) +

  # Texto vertical cerca del punto rojo
  annotate(
    "text",
    x = dose_optimal + 15,
    y = y_optimal + 1.9,
    label = paste0("MCID at ", round(dose_optimal), " METs-min/week"),
    angle = 90, hjust = 0.3, vjust = 0.9,
    color = "red", size = 3.4
  ) +

  # Texto centrado en el área gris
  annotate(
    "text",
    x = (shade_min + shade_max) / 2,
    y = max(pred_curve$fit) + 1.7,
    label = "WHO PA recommendations",
    size = 4.5
  ) +
  
  # Ejes
  labs(
    x = "Physical activity dose (METs-min/week)",
    y = "Estimated change in diastolic blood pressure (Δ mmHg)"
  ) +

  # Tema y tipografía
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    text = element_text(family = "Arial"),
    plot.title = element_text(size = 14, face = "bold")
  )


```


####AG-Dose Response Agent level

##### Estadistico - Dosis Systolic blood pressure

```{r}

# Filtrar agentes válidos (excluye Usual care y Flexibility)
dias.data_agentes <- dias.data %>%
  filter(!trt.2 %in% c("Usual care", "Flexibility"))

# Separar por agente
agente_split_dias <- split(dias.data_agentes, dias.data_agentes$trt.2)

# Loop por agente para mostrar resultados detallados
for (nombre_agente in names(agente_split_dias)) {
  
  datos <- agente_split_dias[[nombre_agente]]
  
  if (nrow(datos) < 5 || length(unique(datos$weekly_dose)) < 4) {
    cat("\n⛔ Agente:", nombre_agente, "- Insuficiente variación o tamaño muestral\n")
    next
  }
  
  cat("\n\n======================================")
  cat("\n📊 Análisis de agente:", nombre_agente)
  cat("\n======================================\n")
  
  # 📌 Modelo lineal simple
  modelo_lin <- lm(y ~ weekly_dose, data = datos)
  cat("\n🔹 Modelo Lineal:\n")
  print(summary(modelo_lin))
  
  # 📈 Comparación con spline (2 df)
  modelo_ns2 <- lm(y ~ ns(weekly_dose, 2), data = datos)
  cat("\n🔸 ANOVA: Lineal vs Spline (2 df):\n")
  print(anova(modelo_lin, modelo_ns2))
  
  # 📈 Comparación con spline (3 df)
  modelo_ns3 <- lm(y ~ ns(weekly_dose, 3), data = datos)
  cat("\n🔸 ANOVA: Lineal vs Spline (3 df):\n")
  print(anova(modelo_lin, modelo_ns3))
  
  # ✅ Clasificación por grupos de dosis
  datos$dose_group <- cut(
    datos$weekly_dose,
    breaks = c(-Inf, 0, 500, 1000, Inf),
    labels = c("Usual Care", "Low", "Medium", "High")
  )
  
  # ⚠️ Validación de número de grupos
  if (length(unique(na.omit(datos$dose_group))) < 2) {
    cat("\n⚠️ No se puede realizar ANOVA categórica (grupos insuficientes)\n")
    next
  }
  
  # 📊 ANOVA categórico
  modelo_cat <- aov(y ~ dose_group, data = datos)
  cat("\n✅ ANOVA por grupo de dosis (categorías):\n")
  print(summary(modelo_cat))
  
  # 🧪 Comparaciones múltiples
  cat("\n🔍 Comparaciones múltiples (Tukey HSD):\n")
  print(TukeyHSD(modelo_cat))
}

```
Ningún agente muestra una relación estadísticamente significativa entre la dosis de ejercicio y el cambio en presión diastólica, al igual que sucedia con la sistolica.

###### Dosis Óptima Systolic blood pressure agent level

Se deja aqui pero al no salir nada significativo en los estadisticos, no merece la pena calcular unos datos y presentarlos. Igualmente dejamos el código para adaptarlo a otros metaánalisis

```{r}

# Filtrar solo agentes activos en diastólica
dias.data_agente <- dias.data %>%
  filter(!trt.2 %in% c("Usual care", "Flexibility"))

# Dividir por agente
split_agente_dias <- split(dias.data_agente, dias.data_agente$trt.2)

# Calcular curva y dosis óptima por agente
optima_agente_dias <- map(split_agente_dias, function(datos) {
  
  if (nrow(datos) < 5 || length(unique(datos$weekly_dose)) < 4) return(NULL)
  
  modelo <- lm(y ~ ns(weekly_dose, 3), data = datos)
  
  dosis_seq <- seq(min(datos$weekly_dose), max(datos$weekly_dose), length.out = 1000)
  predicciones <- predict(modelo, newdata = data.frame(weekly_dose = dosis_seq))
  
  opt_index <- which.min(predicciones)
  opt_dose <- dosis_seq[opt_index]
  opt_resp <- predicciones[opt_index]
  
  grafico <- ggplot(datos, aes(x = weekly_dose, y = y)) +
    geom_point(alpha = 0.5) +
    stat_smooth(method = "lm", formula = y ~ ns(x, 3), col = "blue", se = FALSE) +
    geom_vline(xintercept = opt_dose, linetype = "dashed", color = "red") +
    annotate("text", x = opt_dose, y = min(predicciones),
             label = paste0(round(opt_dose, 0), " MET-min/sem"),
             hjust = -0.1, color = "red") +
    labs(title = paste("Dosis óptima -", unique(datos$trt.2)),
         x = "Dosis semanal (MET-min)", y = "Cambio en presión diastólica (mmHg)") +
    theme_minimal()
  
  list(
    agente = unique(datos$trt.2),
    dosis_optima = round(opt_dose, 1),
    cambio_estimado = round(opt_resp, 2),
    grafico = grafico
  )
})

# Filtrar solo los que tienen resultados válidos
optima_agente_dias <- compact(optima_agente_dias)

# Mostrar tabla resumen
map_dfr(optima_agente_dias, ~tibble(
  agente = .x$agente,
  dosis_optima = .x$dosis_optima,
  cambio_estimado = .x$cambio_estimado
))

optima_agente_dias[["Aerobic"]]$grafico

walk(optima_agente_dias, ~print(.x$grafico))


```

```{r}

# Zona recomendada por la OMS
shade_min <- 600
shade_max <- 1200

# Filtrar agentes activos en diastólica
dias.data_agente <- dias.data %>%
  filter(!trt.2 %in% c("Usual care", "Flexibility"))

# Separar por agente
split_agente_dias <- split(dias.data_agente, dias.data_agente$trt.2)

# Función para curva dosis-respuesta con zona OMS y dosis óptima
grafico_dosis_agente_dias <- map(split_agente_dias, function(df) {
  
  if (nrow(df) < 5 || length(unique(df$weekly_dose)) < 4) return(NULL)
  
  modelo <- lm(y ~ ns(weekly_dose, 3), data = df)
  
  dosis_seq <- seq(min(df$weekly_dose), max(df$weekly_dose), length.out = 1000)
  pred_data <- data.frame(weekly_dose = dosis_seq)
  preds <- predict(modelo, newdata = pred_data, interval = "confidence")
  pred_curve <- cbind(pred_data, preds)
  
  opt_index <- which.min(pred_curve$fit)
  dose_opt <- pred_curve$weekly_dose[opt_index]
  y_opt <- pred_curve$fit[opt_index]
  
  g <- ggplot() +
    geom_rect(aes(xmin = shade_min, xmax = shade_max, ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf),
              fill = "gray70", alpha = 0.2) +
    geom_line(data = pred_curve, aes(x = weekly_dose, y = fit), size = 1) +
    geom_line(data = pred_curve, aes(x = weekly_dose, y = lwr), linetype = "dashed") +
    geom_line(data = pred_curve, aes(x = weekly_dose, y = upr), linetype = "dashed") +
    geom_vline(xintercept = dose_opt, linetype = "dashed", color = "red", linewidth = 0.8) +
    annotate("text", x = dose_opt, y = y_opt,
             label = paste0("Optimal ≈ ", round(dose_opt, 0), " MET-min"),
             vjust = -0.7, hjust = -0.05, color = "red", size = 4) +
    annotate("text", x = (shade_min + shade_max)/2, y = max(pred_curve$fit),
             label = "WHO PA recommendations", vjust = -0.5, size = 4) +
    annotate("text", x = 0, y = min(pred_curve$lwr),
             label = "Model fit:\nSpline (3 df)", hjust = 0, vjust = 0, fontface = "bold") +
    labs(
      title = paste("Dose-response by agent:", unique(df$trt.2)),
      x = "Dose of physical activity (METs-min/week)",
      y = "Estimated effect (Δ diastolic BP)"
    ) +
    theme_minimal()
  
  list(
    agente = unique(df$trt.2),
    dosis_optima = round(dose_opt, 1),
    efecto_optimo = round(y_opt, 2),
    grafico = g
  )
})

plot(rank_probs_sys_trt)
dev.off()
```

#####treatment level_diastolic

Cumulative rank probabilities were also computed.

```{r, collapse=TRUE, fig.height=10, fig.width=15}
# cumulative rank probs
(rank_probs_dias_trt <- posterior_rank_probs(fit_FE_reg_trt_dias, lower_better = TRUE, newdata = tibble(premean = c(75, 85, 90)),
                         study = paste(premean, "mmHg"),
                         cumulative = TRUE))

# plot
tiff("probs_dias_trt.tiff", height = 9, width = 14, units = "in", res = 300)
plot(rank_probs_dias_trt)
dev.off()
```

### Posterior predictive distributions for potential harmful effects

The predictive probability of a new trial showing a harmful effect is:

This model is assuming that there are no differences in risk between different baseline SBP. No se ha calculado

```{r, echo=FALSE}
# predictive distribution
rel_pred <- relative_effects(fit_FE, predictive_distribution = TRUE)
```

```{r}
colMeans(as.matrix(rel_pred) > 0)
```

In the presence of heterogeneity, it has been argued that decision makers should consider the predictive distribution of relative effects in a new study, insted of the posterior distribution of the mean treatment effects, as this reflects uncertainty due to the heterogeneity and may better represent uncertainty about a future roll-out of a treatment. In the unadjusted analysis, whilst there is evidence that some of the modalities are effective on average, and essentially, zero probability of harm based on the mean effect, the predictive distribution for effectiveness in a new study is wide and covers a range of harmful effects.

######Agent level_systolic

For the analysis adjusting for baseline SBP, the predictive distribution of relative effects now depends on baseline SBP; here we calculate these in increments of 5 $mmHg$ from the normal value of SBP (120 $mmHg$).

```{r}
rel_effect_pred_sys_agent <- relative_effects(fit_FE_reg_agent_sys,
                                newdata = tibble::tibble(premean = c(125, 135, 145)),
                                study = premean,
                                predictive_distribution = TRUE)
```

The predicted probabilities of a new trial carried out in participants with different baseline SBP showing a harmful effect can be calculated as:

```{r}
colMeans(as.matrix(rel_effect_pred_sys_agent) > 0)
```

######Agent level_diastolic

```{r}
rel_effect_pred_dias_agent <- relative_effects(fit_FE_reg_agent_dias,
                                newdata = tibble::tibble(premean = c(75, 85, 90)),
                                study = premean,
                                predictive_distribution = TRUE)
```

The predicted probabilities of a new trial carried out in participants with different baseline SBP showing a harmful effect can be calculated as:

```{r}
colMeans(as.matrix(rel_effect_pred_dias_agent) > 0)
```

To introduce an intervention in a specific health context, it is important to predict if no or adverse effects could appear in future trials. We can observe that **aerobic** interventions had associated a quite low probability o showing no or adverse effects for any baseline SBP level. In addition, **mind-body** activities also presented a low probability of adverse effects for people with hypertension in stages 1 or 2.

######Treatment level_systolic

For the analysis adjusting for baseline SBP, the predictive distribution of relative effects now depends on baseline SBP; here we calculate these in increments of 5 $mmHg$ from the normal value of SBP (120 $mmHg$).

```{r}
rel_effect_pred_sys_trt <- relative_effects(fit_FE_reg_trt_sys,
                                newdata = tibble::tibble(premean = c(125, 135, 145)),
                                study = premean,
                                predictive_distribution = TRUE)
```

The predicted probabilities of a new trial carried out in participants with different baseline SBP showing a harmful effect can be calculated as:

```{r}
colMeans(as.matrix(rel_effect_pred_sys_trt) > 0)
```

######Treatment level_diastolic

```{r}
rel_effect_pred_dias_trt <- relative_effects(fit_FE_reg_trt_dias,
                                newdata = tibble::tibble(premean = c(75, 85, 90)),
                                study = premean,
                                predictive_distribution = TRUE)
```

The predicted probabilities of a new trial carried out in participants with different baseline SBP showing a harmful effect can be calculated as:

```{r}
colMeans(as.matrix(rel_effect_pred_dias_trt) > 0)
```

So, for example, the predictive probability that a new trial applying a HIIT carried out in people leaving with T2DM with a baseline SBP of 150 $mmHg$ shows a harmful effect is around 3.43%, whereas applying a running intervention in the same population showing a harmful effect is around 22%. Furthermore, we should take into account that for extreme baseline SBP values, there are not so much information, which could lead to under or over-estimation of harmful effects.
